name: The Name Iran through History
description: Iran has a documented history as a name for people, political territory, and a wider historical homeland. Its adoption in international diplomatic usage in 1935 brought an established internal name into foreign official correspondence.

seo.title: The Name Iran through History | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore the historical meanings of Iran and Eranshahr, their survival in written sources, and the international naming change of 1935.

content.heading: One country, different naming traditions
content.content:
The familiar statement that Persia became Iran in 1935 needs qualification. Historian Yann Richard describes a decision by Reza Shah directing foreign chancelleries—the offices responsible for diplomatic correspondence—to use Iran instead of Persia. The instruction changed international official usage; it did not introduce an unfamiliar name to the country's own historical vocabulary. Richard interprets the decision as part of a deliberate change in how the country presented itself abroad. [s2]

The distinction matters when reading older books and maps. A foreign-language work using Persia may concern the same country that later publications call Iran. Its terminology reflects the conventions of its author and period. The naming decision alone therefore cannot explain changes in the country's government, borders, or population. [s2]

content.heading: People and territory in Sasanian usage
content.content:
The clearest early evidence comes from the Sasanian dynasty. Linguist D. N. MacKenzie identifies Ērān in the titles of its founder, Ardashir I, on a relief at Naqsh-e Rostam in Fars and on his coins. The underlying word initially referred to Iranians as a people. MacKenzie explains its derivation from an older Iranian plural form; the historical term sometimes translated as Aryan must be understood in that ancient linguistic context. [s1]

Under Ardashir's son Shapur I, Ērānšahr appears in a royal inscription. MacKenzie distinguishes this designation for the empire from Ērān as a designation for its people, while showing that the shorter word also acquired geographical meaning early. He cautions that the compound Ērānšahr is not attested in the Old Persian inscriptions of the earlier Achaemenid dynasty. [s1]

content.heading: A name whose geographical meaning changed
content.content: Later Middle Persian books preserved these terms, and early New Persian writing used forms including Ērānšahr and shahr-e Ērān. Their geographical meanings were not fixed: MacKenzie traces changes in the territory described and records Iran and Iranzamin as broader designations for the land of Iranians. Historical uses consequently need to be read in their own textual setting rather than plotted automatically onto today's borders. [s1]

content.heading: Iran and Persian describe different things
content.content: The country's name should also be distinguished from the name of a language. The Library of Congress identifies Persian as an Iranian branch language of the Indo-European family and notes the regional names Farsi, Dari, and Tajiki. Its account describes a literary tradition extending across Iran, Central Asia, and South Asia. Calling the country Iran therefore does not require replacing Persian as the English language name, nor does Persian literature fit exclusively within the boundaries of the modern state. [s3]

name: National & Local Identities
description: Iranian belonging can coexist with affiliations rooted in language, locality, kinship, and cultural practice. These connections overlap, but neither a language label nor a regional origin fully describes an individual's identity.

seo.title: National & Local Identities in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: How national belonging, local attachments, languages, and shared celebrations intersect across Iran without forming a single uniform identity.

content.heading: Belonging at more than one scale
content.content:
National and local identities in Iran are best approached as overlapping affiliations. Encyclopaedia Iranica describes kinship, tribal connections, language, religion, and provincial attachments alongside an overarching Iranian identity. Its account also recognizes competition between these allegiances. Shared belonging should therefore not be assumed to remove differences or disagreements. [s1]

The same essay identifies historical memory and cultural heritage, especially Persian literature, as important sources of cohesion. This is a scholarly interpretation of how a shared identity has been sustained, rather than a measurement of what every Iranian feels. It also describes identity as repeatedly reconstructed through history. A useful reading leaves room for change: attachment to a locality and attachment to a country need not have the same meaning in every period. [s1]

content.heading: Why language is not a complete identity map
content.content:
Language provides an important connection to a community, but it does not act as a complete inventory of belonging. Gernot Windfuhr's overview distinguishes language, ethnicity, and culture as different, overlapping networks. He illustrates cultural layering through personal names drawn from Iranian, Arabic, Turkic, and European traditions. A name may preserve a historical connection or reflect a new cultural choice without identifying everything about its bearer. [s2]

Place names introduce another layer. They can retain traces of earlier populations, migrations, or deliberate renaming long after their original meaning becomes obscure. Windfuhr consequently emphasizes careful historical and linguistic analysis. A familiar-sounding name alone is insufficient evidence for claims about the ancestry or present identity of everyone living there. For readers, the practical lesson is to distinguish the history of a word from the self-description of a person. [s2]

content.heading: Shared celebrations can cross national boundaries
content.content:
Nowruz, the celebration marking spring and renewal, offers a concrete example of cultural connections operating across scales. UNESCO describes family meals, visits, new clothing, and gift-giving among its practices. It also places the celebration across a broad geographical area, including the Caucasus, Central Asia, and the Middle East. Participation in such a tradition can connect a household to a wider cultural world without making that world a single nationality. [s3]

UNESCO's account emphasizes intergenerational solidarity and relationships between communities. These are the values highlighted by its heritage description; they should not be read as proof that every celebration has identical customs or achieves the same social outcomes. The example is useful because it shows how a recognizable shared occasion can extend beyond the boundaries of one state. [s3]

content.heading: Read identities without turning them into fixed boxes
content.content: Taken together, these sources suggest an approach based on context. Ask whether a label concerns language, family history, locality, or a wider historical community. Avoid treating one answer as a substitute for all the others. This is an editorial synthesis of the sources, rather than a survey finding: overlapping affiliations help explain cultural connections, while leaving individuals room to describe the importance of those connections for themselves. [s1][s2][s3]

name: Languages & Dialects
description: Iran's linguistic landscape includes Persian and other Iranian languages alongside Turkic, Semitic, and additional language traditions. Language families, regional varieties, and multilingual practices provide different ways to understand this diversity.

seo.title: Languages & Dialects of Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: An introduction to Persian, other Iranian languages, Turkic varieties, Arabic, and Iran's multilingual landscape.

content.heading: Languages of Iran and Iranian languages
content.content:
Two similar expressions describe different things. Languages of Iran is a geographical description. Iranian languages is a classification based on descent from a shared ancestral language. Prods Oktor Skjærvø's linguistic overview places the Iranian group within Indo-Iranian, itself a branch of Indo-European. Its members are spoken both inside and far beyond Iran. Persian is one member of this group; the group is not simply a collection of Persian dialects. [s1]

This distinction helps explain why the language map cannot be reduced to national borders. Kurdish and Balochi, for example, have distributions extending into neighboring countries. Within Iran, Gilaki and Mazandarani belong to the Caspian linguistic landscape, while Luri and Bakhtiari varieties are discussed among the languages of western and southwestern Iran. Talysh is associated with the western Caspian area. These regional descriptions indicate broad distributions, not exclusive territories. [s1]

content.heading: Persian connects several literary worlds
content.content: Persian has a geographical reach wider than Iran. The Library of Congress uses Persian as the established English name and identifies Farsi, Dari, and Tajiki as regional names. Its exhibition describes a literary culture extending through Central Asia and into South Asia, including settings associated with the Mughal and Ottoman empires. This wider history helps readers understand why Persian texts, authors, and artistic traditions cannot always be assigned exclusively to one modern nation. [s2]

content.heading: Turkic languages have their own internal geography
content.content:
Turkic languages form another important part of Iran's linguistic landscape. Windfuhr distinguishes the Oghuz varieties from Khalaj, which constitutes a separate Turkic branch. His survey includes Azerbaijani, Qashqai, Khorasan Turkish, and Turkmen, as well as smaller regional varieties. These are not branches of Persian. [s3]

Even a familiar label contains local distinctions. The survey describes Azerbaijani varieties associated with Tabriz, Urmia, Ardabil, and Zanjan. It places Qashqai within southern Oghuz and discusses Turkmen in the northeast. Such distinctions make a broad language label useful as an entry point rather than a complete description of an individual speaker's speech. The classification is linguistic; it should not be treated as a direct statement about a person's nationality or political affiliation. [s3]

content.heading: The landscape extends beyond Iranian and Turkic
content.content:
Other traditions complicate any two-part picture. Windfuhr's survey identifies Arabic and Neo-Aramaic within the Semitic group, Armenian within Indo-European, Georgian, and Brahui within Dravidian. His historical account also describes Arabic and Turkic influences on Persian and other languages, including vocabulary and grammatical features. Contact is therefore part of the history of the languages themselves, not just an encounter between otherwise isolated communities. [s4]

Arabic illustrates why regional detail matters. Windfuhr discusses varieties in Khuzestan and the Persian Gulf region alongside smaller, historically documented communities farther east. He relates Khuzestan Arabic to the dialect continuum of Iraq. Remembered Arab ancestry and continued Arabic speech do not always coincide: his account explicitly describes communities that retained an origin label after language shift. [s5]

content.heading: Read a language map alongside social context
content.content:
Windfuhr describes bilingualism and multilingualism as common in many regions and emphasizes intersecting cultural, ethnic, and linguistic affiliations. A map showing a language in a locality consequently does not establish that every resident speaks only that language. It also does not measure proficiency, the language used in a particular setting, or the importance a speaker gives it. Those questions require more specific evidence. [s4]

The pages in this branch therefore separate major language traditions from the study of local varieties. They offer starting points for understanding relationships and regional distinctions. A responsible overview preserves those distinctions while acknowledging that the sources inspected here do not establish current speaker totals or a complete inventory of every locality. [s1][s3][s4]
